sn47.2:1.1: This is an excerpt from the narrative at [dn16:2.11.5](); see too [sn36.7]().
sn47.2:2.1: _Sampajāna_ (“aware”, rendered in its noun form as “situational awareness”) is linguistically similar to _paññā_ (“wisdom”). However it is used in context as a pragmatic understanding, not liberating insight (see also [dn9:17.9](), [mn122:9.5]()).
sn47.2:3.2: “Situational awareness” (_sampajañña_) understands the context and purpose of activities. The main examples here illustrate the activities of daily monastic life: leaving the monastery on almsround, restraint while in the town, care wearing the robes, then mindfully eating and going to the toilet. Situational awareness is, alternatively, described as the meditative practice of being aware of thoughts, feelings, and perceptions ([sn47.35]()). | This passage was included in the Satipaṭṭhānasutta at [mn10:8.1]().
sn47.2:3.3: Rather unusually, in this trope there is a different phrasing for the opening, where they are “aware” (_sampajāno_) and closing, where they are an “aware-actor” (_sampajānakārī_).
